The chronicles tells us that when Grand Prince Vladimir ascended the throne to the realm that would later to become known to us as Russia in the year 980, he initiated an inquiry about all the known religions and examined them in a new decree which he himself supervised. Vladimir believed his new and modern state deserved a modern religion.

He favored islam but due to its various taboos, of alcohol specifically, it was cut completely out of the question: "Drinking is the joy of the Russians - we cannot live without that pleasure."

Judaism was rejected as well; the loss of Jerusalem was clear evidence that the judean god had forsaken his followers. He then dispatched commissions to the christian areas throughout Europe. Roman Catholisism was perhaps accecptable, but the sermons, however, were uneventful and boring. Nearly all of the candidate religions were now exhausted, but on their journey home the emissaries had visited Constantinople and they told their monarch:

Vladimir listened in astonishment, and consequently Russia adopted the Orthodox Christianity. Both the Greek faith and the Greek alphabet has been kept to this day. -End of digression-

At May 29, 1453 Constantinople was conquered by the muslims. This meant the end of the Byzantine Empire. This day symbolizes the decisive defeat on the eastern flank of christianity. Some historians also mark this event as the end of the medieval period. On the Turkish side, Osman emerged as as a warrior king, with an army organized in guilds and inspired by a mystic branch of Islam. The Osmans' (or the Ottomans') conquests swept quickly and efficiently throughout the territories of Anatolia and the Middle East. Osman's son took the title "Sultan", and established a special corps for fighting in Europe, the janissaries. The janissary corps was composed of christian children abducted from their families as infants, raised as muslims and trained for combat. The Sultan army conquered the Balkans, Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece. In the mid-1400's their leader was Mehmet II.

In this turbulent age the emperor of the Byzantines traveled to the courts of kings and emperors throughout Europe begging for help against the growing Turkish threat. He didn't recieve much aid though.

When Sultan Mehmet was recognized as the leader of the Ottoman Empire, he suspects his younger brother might become a rival to his rule. Mehmet hires a man to drown him in the bath, and shortly thereafter kills the assassin himself. Mehmet has vowed to conquer Byzantium. Reports from outlying sources tell that he has supernatural capabilities, that he is an intellectual who reads the writings of Caesar in its original latin, and a barbarian who will spill blood without any hesitation. He has got melancholic eyes and a nose like the beak of a parrot, he works tirelessly, and lacks conscience completely.

Of the Byzantine Empire there are now just parts of the capital city left; pillaged by crusaders, depopulated by plague. But the most splendid church of all, Hagia Sofia, still remains the centre of christian faith.

The emperor is begging the military powers of Western Europe for galleys and soldiers. But no response. The Greek church despises the Roman church, and now it wants their help! The emperor is desperate and with the imminent Turkish danger on all borders, the Eastern Church finally recognizes the Pope as the true leader of Christianity.

Byzantium bows for Rome. The name of the Pope is for the first time included in the prayers of the Eastern Church. After all these years of schism, finally reconciliation.

The Ottoman army rides across the plains towards the city walls. Leading them is the twenty-one year old Sultan wearing magnificent clothes. The strength of Byzantium is its solid walls and parapets, turrets and moats in a multi-layered defence. No other city in Europe has stronger bulwark. But Mehmet's freshly cast siege mortars are slowly chewing their way through the fortifications. Within the city walls, women are kneeling at the shrines with their children gathered around them:

"The Western Church has promised to help us; when will the Venetian fleet be here?"

Four Genovese ships arrive. The besieged Greeks believes this is the onset of a counterstrike. But no more ships arrive. The theological disagreements are still too great for the West to help cordially. The battle is set; Byzantium is being defended by eight thousand men, against the enemy's one hundred and fifty thousand. The great onslaught is set for Tuesday, May 29. The roar "Plunder!" is heard from the sieging soldiers, sung in rhythm and cheer.

Within the walls, the emperor calls for the icons being gathered from the churches and brought in procession through the streets. Then, the condemned gather in Hagia Sofia for a ceremony of ecstasy. The patriarch uplifts his voice in a mighty appeal, the light of a thousand candles banishes the darkness from their sanctuary, the voices of the choir sound more beautiful than ever. The emperor steps up to the altar. The withered Eastern Roman Empire is gathered for her own requiem.

When the 29th of May is one hour old, the signal of attack is heard. The defenders fight bravely, still protected by heavy walls, although with cracks. The Sultan's attacking divisions are being replaced, and replaced again. The third surge is composed of twelve thousand well-rested janissaries. But Byzanthium holds firm. For a few hours the city seems impenetrable.

It is at this point two Turkish soldiers discover this small, insignificant gate in the inner wall the defenders have forgotten to close. The janissaries rush over. One platoon manages to get through, some of the defenders on the walls recognize enemy troops behind their own ranks and cry out in despair:

"The city has fallen!"

The news spread like wildfire, the defense crumbles. The emperor and some of his most loyal men takes up a final, desperate fight against the attackers. But the emperor falls in battle without anyone realizing who he is. The following day his body is found in a pile of corpses; identified by his purple dyed shoes, which is decorated with a golden eagle.

The city of Byzantium was founded at some point around 650 B.C. by seafarers from Megara. A thousand years later it was renamed Constantinople, and today it's called Istanbul. The Byzantine Empire came to an end. Everything supposedly impenetrable has somewhere got a small and insignificant little crack which somebody has forgotten to seal.

A handful of things:

  • /v/Introductions is a great place to start for new accounts
  • get into the habit of using the "preview" button before you submit a comment - it's a rad feature
  • Voat has open mod logs so every moderator action is tracked; they're linked at the bottom of each sub's sidebar
  • if you're in the habit of submitting links and providing an archive link in the comments, I've got a handy bookmarklet for that
  • /v/all is pretty active, so check out /v/all/new if you're looking for active subverses to subscribe to
  • Voat's web design is nicer looking than Reddit's; night mode can be even easier on the eyes. Toggle that with the lightbulb in the top right
  • you can block subverses you don't want to see by going to that subverse and choosing "block" or clicking on the "block subverse" link when viewing a post in /v/all. Voat puts filtering controls in the hands of the users; it doesn't decide what lawful content to quarantine for you.

Some people are helpful and some people are jerks, just like out in the real world. Be who you want to be and welcome to the community!

Edit: forgot to mention, /v/Whatever is a great resource for "catch-all" content that doesn't really fit anywhere else. It's kept /v/pics and /v/news from becoming the defacto catch-all subs and has a lot of interesting content of its own.
